paragraphs.text: Lesson 2, which restaurant?
Nate and Andrew are two army soldiers who are trying to decide where to eat on their days off.
First, listen to their conversation and try to answer the comprehension questions.
Mmm, mmm. I can't wait to order a huge plate of those sweet and sour noodles.
I've been craving Chinese food for the past week.
No way, man. We're gonna have some Italian food.
If I don't get some of the lasagna pronto, I'm gonna have a fit.
You and your lasagna. Didn't your mom just make lasagna when you went home for a visit?
Nah, she stuffed me full of Thai food. Not that I'm complaining.
The food was good and all, but I really had my heart set on some lasagna.
Come on, Andrew. You have to be fair. I've been eating army food for months now.
At least you got to go home last weekend.
Hey, you're the one that got busted and had your leaf taken away.
What were you thinking sneaking chocolate bars into the barracks anyway?
Forget about the chocolate bars. I'm talking Chinese food at Mr. Chen's restaurant.
Alright, alright. Chill out. Here's what we'll do.
We have two days leave, right?
Yeah, two days.
Okay, so here's the plan. Today, we'll hit Mr. Chen's Chinese buffet and eat till we burst.
And then tomorrow, we'll go to an Italian restaurant for a plate of steaming hot lasagna.
You know what? Now that I think about it, the Italian place is closer to the base than Mr. Chen's.
It's cool if we stop there first.
Nah, no worries, man. My lasagna can wait. I've actually been never been to Mr. Chen's.
You haven't? Oh, you are in for a treat.
I don't know what kind of secret sauce he uses, but the noodles are addictive.
Sure beats army food, huh?
When I went home last week and I popped into an old burger joint where I used to hang out with my buddies.
The burgers were swimming in Greece, but after eating army food, they were like a taste of heaven.
Well now my stomach's rumbling! Let's get out of here and get some grub.
Watch out, Mr. Chen. Here come two hungry soldiers.
Let's learn the vocabulary from the conversation about restaurants.
Nate says, I've been craving Chinese food for the past week.
Craving means strongly desiring.
It's often used for food, although it can be used for other things too.
Andrew says, no way, man.
No way is an informal way to say no or definitely not.
Then Andrew says, if I don't get some lasagna pronto, I'm going to have a fit.
Pronto is a slang word that means very fast or very soon.
And I'm going to have a fit means I'm going to become very upset.
Andrew says he had his heart set on some lasagna.
To have your heart set on something means to especially want something special.
You have a desire for one specific thing.
You have your heart set on it.
Unfortunately, Nate got busted.
Got busted is a slang term.
It means he got caught doing something bad and got in trouble.
His punishment was to have his leave taken away.
Leave, in this case, is actually a noun.
It refers to the period of time that members of the military have off.
They have free time during which they can leave the military base and go home or travel.
Andrew asks Nate, what were you thinking sneaking chocolate bars into the barracks anyway?
Sneaking means doing something in secret.
And the word barracks refers to the place where members of the military live.
So sneaking chocolate bars into the barracks means that Nate secretly took chocolate bars
into the military residential rooms.
Nate insists that they should go for Chinese food and Andrew says,
alright, alright, chill out.
Chill out is a phrasal verb meaning to relax or calm down.
Andrew then makes a plan.
Next, will hit Mr. Chen's Chinese buffet.
Hit in this context means go to a place.
This is an informal slang word.
Some people say, for example, let's hit the bar after work.
That means let's go to the bar after work.
A buffet is a restaurant where you can serve yourself from a large selection of foods.
Note that the T at the end of buffet is silent.
And the expression eat till we burst means eat a lot until we can't eat anymore.
Nate says the Italian place is closer to the base than Mr. Chen's.
The word base refers to the military area.
Then Nate says, it's cool if we stop there first.
It's cool means it's okay.
And Andrew responds, nah, no worries, man.
No worries means no problem or don't worry about it.
When Andrew says he's never been to Mr. Chen's restaurant, Nate says, ahh, you're in for a treat.
You're in for a treat means you will have a special wonderful experience.
Andrew replies, sure beats army food, huh?
Beats means is better than.
He's saying that restaurant food is better than army food.
When Andrew went home last weekend, he popped into an old burger joint.
Popped into is an informal phrasal verb meaning quickly stopped inside a place.
Andrew says an old burger joint.
Joint is slang for restaurant.
It's a place where he used to hang out with his buddies.
Buddies is a slang word for friends.
Then he describes the food.
The burgers were swimming in Greece.
Swimming in Greece means extremely greasy or oily.
Nate says, well now my stomach's rumbling.
Rumbling means making low noises.
Things that rumble include your stomach when you are hungry.
Thunder during a thunderstorm and an earthquake can also produce a rumbling sound.
Then Nate says, let's get out of here and get some grub.
Grub is a slang word for food.
And it's usually only used in this expression.
Let's get some grub.
That's all the vocabulary from today's conversation.
Go ahead and try the vocabulary quiz to put these expressions into practice.
And the speaking task to get some feedback on your spoken English.
